thread.title: Apple Plunges Into A Bear Market: 4 Things Investors Need To Know - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Dividend Sensei
title: Apple Plunges Into A Bear Market: 4 Things Investors Need To Know - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
(Source: imgflip )
Historically, there have been two time-tested methods for long-term investors to achieve strong, market-beating returns that can help them achieve their financial goals over time. The first is buying quality dividend growth stocks which have been the best performing asset class in history.
Since 1972, not just have dividend growth stocks beaten the market by 31% annually, but they’ve done so with 13% less volatility, thus achieving 51% better annualized risk-adjusted returns.
The second is to buy these quality companies at a good price, meaning fair value or better. A Yale study found that, between 1881 and 2016, the starting PE at which you bought a stock affected total returns out to 30 years.
Thus, my goal is always to find good dividend growth ideas for readers (and myself) trading at fair value or better. Thus, when blue-chip dividend growth stocks fall into a bear market, my contrarian value ears perk up, because I know that such times are the best opportunities for adding Grade A dividend growth stocks to your portfolio.
Apple ( AAPL ), long a darling of Wall Street, is the latest high flying tech name to fall into a bear market. But given that the company is still up 15% for the year, many investors are understandably confused about whether or not the stock is a strong buy at today’s prices, or potentially set to fall far even further.
So, let’s take a look at four things investors need to know about Apple’s recent plunge. Specifically why Wall Street has turned so sour on the company, what the market is likely missing, and why Apple remains one of the top long-term dividend growth blue chips you can own over the coming decade. Most importantly, find out why Apple is likely a decent, though not necessarily great buy, at today’s much lower prices. That’s because, it’s likely between -11% and 3% undervalued, but that should still be capable of delivering about 14% long-term annualized total returns in the coming decade.
1. Why Wall Street Freaked Out Over Apple’s Earnings Given the violent negative reaction in the share price, one might think that Apple’s latest earnings results were horrible. In fact, that couldn’t be further from the truth.

The company actually posted 20% revenue growth in the final quarter of its fiscal year, the fastest growth rate in three years.
(Source: earnings release)
That was largely driven by three things. The most notable was the 29% increase in iPhone revenue, which was entirely a result of the average selling price of ASP rising to $793 from Q3’s 2017’s $618. That was due to the launch of much more expensive iPhones this year (prices as high as $1,450 per phone).
Yet despite the much higher prices, Apple continues to delight its customers. Here’s what CFO Luca Maestri told analysts on the last conference call:
“The latest survey of US consumers from 451 Research indicates customer satisfaction of 98% for iPhone X, iPhone 8 and iPhone 8 Plus combined , and among business buyers who plan to purchase smartphones in the December quarter, 80% plan to purchase iPhones . ” - Luca Maestri (emphasis added)
The other key growth drivers were services and “other products” which is mostly the company’s wearables (Apple Watch) and HomePod speaker (over 50% YOY growth). Not just did these segments post strong growth, but together accounted for 23% of company sales, showing that Apple is making good progress in diversifying its business from its overreliance on the iPhone. So if Apple’s results were so strong, and set yet another record for the company, then why has the share price been tanking?
What freaked out Wall Street was Q4 guidance growth that implied just 3% revenue growth at the mid-range. That’s a far cry from the very impressive figures Apple has been posting all year and the 16% revenue growth analysts expect in 2018. Many investors assume this means that “peak iPhone” sales will ultimately mean much slower growth in the future. About 2% of that slower top-line growth in Q4 will be due to the stronger dollar.
Those growth fears have been stoked in recent weeks by analysts speculating that iPhone sales in Apple’s holiday quarter are going to be much weaker than previously expected. That speculation was triggered by Lumentum Holdings ( LITE ), a key Apple supplier cutting its Q4 guidance citing “a request from one of our largest Industrial and Consumer customers for laser diodes for 3D sensing to materially reduce shipments to them during our fiscal second quarter for previously placed orders that were originally scheduled for delivery during the quarter." While Apple wasn’t specifically mentioned, Wall Street has a long history of jumping to conclusions about supplier delivery cuts meaning that iPhone shipments are in trouble.
Ming-Chi Kuo, a respected analyst with TF International Securities recently slashed his forecast for Q4 iPhone volumes from 100 million to 70 million . That’s largely a result of two factors. The first is the trade war with China that is expected to hurt iPhone sales in the Middle Kingdom. On top of that Kuo is worried about rising competition from rival and lower cost products such as Huawei's Mate 20 series. Add to this that Apple’s strong emerging market growth is expected to take a hit thanks to the rising US dollar, which is largely being driven by rising US interest rates and stronger growth relative to other developed economies.
“The emerging markets that we are seeing pressure in our markets like Turkey, India, Brazil, Russia. These are markets where currencies have weakened over the recent period, in some cases that resulted in us raising prices and those markets are not growing the way we would like to see.” - Tim Cook
Finally, investors were spooked by management announcing it would no longer be breaking out unit sales for any of its iOS products, including the iPhone. Management said that this was because:
“As demonstrated by our financial performance in recent years, the number of units sold in any 90-day period is not necessarily representative of the underlying strength of our business. Furthermore, a unit of sale is less relevant for us today than it was in the past given the breadth of our portfolio and the wider sales price dispersion within any given product line…. if you look at our revenue during the last three years, if you look at our net income during the last three years, if you look at our stock price in the last three years, there is no correlation to the units sold in any given period. ” - Luca Maestri (emphasis added)
While what Mrs. Maestri says is objectively true, long unit obsessed Wall Street still sees the lack of future unit disclosure as a negative, fearing that Apple has “something to hide”. But the reason I remain bullish about Apple is that I consider Wall Street’s fears to be overblown and expect the company to continue to deliver double-digit bottom line and dividend growth in the coming years.
2. What The Street Is Missing There are three reasons why I’m not at all worried about Apple’s ability to generate strong growth in the future. First, as Apple’s CFO pointed out, Apple’s iPhone unit volumes peaking has not hurt the company.
iPhone Unit Volumes By Quarter
(Source: Statista )
First, let’s not forget that iPhone unit volumes peaked many quarters ago, back in Q1 2017 (at 78.3 million). Since that time, Apple’s fundamentals have all improved steadily.
(Source: Ycharts)
Ultimately, what matters to investors is the fundamentals which mean EPS, FCF/share and dividends. As long as those continue rising steadily, it doesn’t matter how Apple achieves that positive growth.
Next, we can’t forget that Apple’s long-term growth strategy isn’t predicated on steadily growing iPhone unit volumes, but rather monetizing its sticky walled garden iOS ecosystem. That ecosystem’s moat remains wide, courtesy of those industry-leading customer satisfaction and loyalty figures. For instance, according to analyst firm, Fluent 80% of iPhone owners planned to buy another iPhone with 70% of survey respondents saying they wouldn’t even consider another phone.
Apple plans to convert the 1.3 billion user base of iOS devices into an ever larger number of paid subscribers that can generate a steady stream of lucrative revenue and cash flow in the future.
(Source: Motley Fool )
Over the past two years, Apple has done a remarkable job of growing its subscriber base which has allowed its service revenue to continue growing at over 20% per year. Those subscriptions are across the company’s wide suite of services which include App Store, Cloud Services, Apple care, Apple Music and Apple Pay. In the last quarter, paid subscriptions rose 50% YOY compared to Q3 2017, despite an already enormous user base.
(Source: earnings releases)
And keep in mind that in Q3 2018 service revenue growth would have been 27% had it not been for a one-time accounting benefit in Q3 2017 that added $640 million to that quarter’s figure. This basically means that Apple’s service business, which represents highly stable and lucrative recurring revenue, continues to grow at an impressive clip, despite its $40 billion annual run rate.
(Source: earnings releases)
In fact, management had previously said it wanted to hit $50 billion in service revenue by 2020. In the past 12 months, service revenue was $37.2 billion, and since early 2015, Apple’s service revenue growth has averaged 19%. That puts the company well ahead of its already ambitious service revenue goal. Here’s how that business unit will look over the coming years if Apple can maintain that average growth rate (which is significantly slower than in recent quarters).

Why do I believe that Apple can maintain that kind of service growth rate? Because the service business has its finger in numerous strong growth opportunities, including mobile payments.
“I want to spotlight the exceptional performance of Apple Pay which is by far the number one mobile contactless payment service worldwide. Transaction volume tripled year-over-year. And to put that into perspective, Apple Pay generated significantly more transactions than even PayPal Mobile with over four times the growth rate. ” Tim Cook, (emphasis added)
Thus, I consider Apple to be a great, low-risk way of investing in the “death of cash” where convenience and incredible loyalty from the iOS userbase gives Apple Pay a major competitive advantage over smaller rivals.
Ultimately, what matters to Apple shareholders is whether or not the company’s earnings and cash flow per share (and dividends) can keep growing. As you can see, analysts currently expect the company to continue delivering double-digit growth in the coming years.

That’s despite a slowdown in revenue growth to the mid-single (4% to 7%) digits. How can Apple deliver on those expectations? That would be because the company remains committed to its epic cash return program, including the most aggressive share buyback program in history ($239 billion so far).
(Source: Apple )
Remember that Apple has said they want to get to a net cash position of zero, and currently, the net cash position sits at $123 billion. And Apple’s mountain of net cash is hardly the only thing that will be fueling its buybacks. Over the past 12 months, the company generated $64 billion in free cash flow and, after paying the dividend, retained FCF was $50 billion.
(Source: Ycharts)
Since it started return cash to shareholders Apple’s share count has fallen by 6.2% CAGR, and in Q3, that accelerated to 6.5%. With the share price now down significantly in recent weeks, we can probably expect Apple to accelerate its repurchases a bit in Q4. After all, in Q2 2018, which was during the last stock market correction, the company repurchased $23.5 billion in shares. But won’t Apple eventually run out of net cash to fund those massive buybacks? Sure, but assuming $20 billion in repurchases per quarter, and no growth in retained FCF, that would take about six quarters to accomplish. Over that time, Apple’s post-dividend free cash flow would likely allow it to repurchase an additional $75 billion in stock for a total of $198 billion in buybacks, and lower its share count another 20%.
The bottom line is that while Apple’s days of double-digit revenue growth are likely behind it, the company’s overall business model remains as strong as ever. The super loyal customer base, which management is converting into an army of service subscribers, means that Apple is likely to remain a free cash flow minting machine. One that continues to present one of the most attractive long-term dividend profiles on Wall Street, which means marketing-beating double-digit total returns are likely to continue for many years to come.
3. Dividend Profile: Apple Is Still A Great Dividend Stock With Double-Digit Long-Term Return Potential The most important thing for any income investments is the dividend profile which consists of three parts: yield, dividend safety, and long-term payout growth potential (a proxy for earnings and cash flow growth). Combined with valuation, this is what typically determines total returns.

Even after its 20% decline from its recent all-time highs Apple’s yield is not anything to get excited about. But what it lacks in current income Apple more than makes up for in dividend safety and long-term growth potential. That’s courtesy of a very low FCF payout ratio of just 21% over the past year. That means that Apple is retaining $50 billion in FCF after paying its dividend and could easily grow the dividend at a mid to high-double-digit rate for many years to come.
The second part of the dividend safety equation is the balance sheet.

Even factoring in the company’s $114 billion debt load, Apple’s leverage ratio remains well below the industry average. And the sky-high interest coverage ratio shows that Apple has no problem servicing that low-cost debt. Apple’s average interest rate is actually slightly lower than the US Treasury’s (2.9%) even before factoring in the interest deductibility it still enjoys under current US tax law. That’s thanks to one of the strongest credit ratings in corporate America. And of course, we can’t forget that since Apple actually has a net cash position of $123 billion, the actual leverage metrics are pretty much a moot point. Apple’s dividend is, simply put, one of the safest on Wall Street, and likely to keep growing at a rapid clip for the foreseeable future.
How fast? Well, that depends on how management wants to structure its future capital return program. Tim Cook has said that Apple will raise its dividend every year, though he hasn’t indicated how quickly. But since it restarted its dividend in late 2012, Apple’s payout has grown at 11.5% CAGR . For my return model, I assume that Apple will maintain the currently very low FCF payout ratio in order to maximize retained FCF that it can funnel into its massive buyback program.
But even that would mean that Apple’s dividend would likely grow in line with EPS (and FCF/share) which analysts currently expect to increase at 13.1% CAGR over the next decade. Combined with that modest yield, that would mean that Apple’s shares should deliver about 14.6% total returns over time. That’s based on the Gordon Dividend Growth Model or GDGM which has proven relatively effective for forecasting total returns for companies since 1956. The GDGM says that over time total returns track yield + long-term EPS/FCF/dividend growth. The model assumes that valuation changes cancel out over time because over many years, a stock’s share price is purely a function of its earnings, cash flow and dividends (the fundamentals).
Even adjusting for Apple’s range of valuations (from slightly undervalued to slightly overvalued), I estimate that Apple is likely to deliver long-term CAGR total returns of 13.5% to 14.9%. For context, the S&P 500 has historically delivered 9.2% CAGR total returns and from current valuations, I expect just 8.3% long-term returns from the market. That might be overly generous given that BlackRock, Morningstar and Vanguard’s founder Jack Bogle expect the market to deliver anywhere from 0% to 5% CAGR total returns over the coming five to 10 years.
The bottom line is that Apple remains a world-class dividend growth stock, one that’s likely to deliver strong double-digit bottom line and dividend growth in the coming years. That should allow it to remain a market-beating stock and well worth owning in most income growth portfolios.
But that being said, despite its recent plunge, I don’t consider Apple a “very strong” buy for new money today. That’s because, while certainly much improved in recent weeks, the stock is arguably very close to fair value or even potentially slightly overvalued.
4. Valuation: Not Necessarily A Screaming Bargain But Potentially A Good Buy Now
(Source: Ycharts)
Even with the recent bear market Apple has managed to deliver solid total returns over the past year, far in excess of the S&P 500 and most tech stocks. But that brings up the question of just how good of a place is Apple for new money today? That’s not necessarily easy to answer since there are dozens of ways to potentially value a company. But to help you decide whether Apple is a good buy for you, here are three approaches that have historically proven useful for blue-chips like this.
The first is to look at the company’s PE ratio and compare it to its historical norms.

Apple is trading at 16.3 times trailing earnings compared to 22.3 for the S&P 500. On a forward PE basis, Apple appears pretty cheap at just 14.4, which is compared to 17.3 for most tech companies and in line with its own five year forward PE average of 14.0. More importantly, that trailing PE ratio implies that just 3.9% long-term EPS growth is baked into the stock. Even if you don’t agree with analysts that Apple will be able to achieve 13% long-term growth, buybacks alone will be enough to clear that very low bar. That implies that Apple is indeed undervalued, or at very least close to fair value.
To confirm this, I often turn to Morningstar’s three-stage discounted cash flow or DCF model. That’s because Morningstar analysts are 100% long-term fundamental focused and usually use more conservative growth assumptions than most analysts.

Today, Morningstar estimates that Apple is worth $200 per share or about 3% undervalued. That means a very modest long-term (10 years) valuation boost that could allow Apple to deliver about 15% long-term total returns.
One final valuation model I consider, and the one that is by far my favorite for blue-chip dividend growth stocks, is called dividend yield theory or DYT. This has proven highly accurate for stable business model companies like Apple since 1966. That’s when the asset manager/newsletter publisher Investment Quality Trends began using DYT exclusively to generate decades of market-beating returns. This is over every time frame, and with about 10% less volatility to boot.
(Source: Investment Quality Trends)
DYT simply says that a dividend stock’s yield tends to be stable and mean reverting over time. This means cycling around a long-term historical average that approximates fair value. Comparing the yield to the fair value yield can give you an idea of how under/overvalued a dividend stock might be, and thus how much of long-term valuation boost you’ll get from the yield returning to its historical norm over time.

Unfortunately, that higher yield means that Apple might still be overvalued, by about 11%. The good news is that over time that will likely cause the shares to appreciate just 1.1% CAGR slower than EPS/FCF/dividends. This ultimately means that Apple could be anywhere from 11% overvalued to 3% undervalued, and thus investors can likely expect between 13.5% and 14.9% long-term total returns.
For a Grade A blue chip like this, that’s still strong enough that I can recommend shares at today’s prices. But for my own portfolio (which targets higher total returns) I’m personally waiting for Apple to hit my target yield of 1.8%.
But of course, anyone buying Apple today needs to be comfortable with its risk profile.
Risks To Consider For an in-depth look at Apple’s fundamental risks see this article (non-paywalled).
For this article, I’m going to address the stock’s recent volatility and merely point out that like all great companies, Apple is not immune from the intrinsic forces of creative destruction that are the hallmark of capitalism.
“Amazon is not too big to fail… In fact, I predict one day Amazon will fail. Amazon will go bankrupt. If you look at large companies, their lifespans tend to be 30-plus years, not hundred-plus years...If we start to focus on ourselves, instead of focusing on our customers, that will be the beginning of the end...We have to try and delay that day for as long as possible." - Jeff Bezos (emphasis added)
This quote from Amazon ( AMZN ) founder and CEO Jeff Bezos highlights how even the most dominant companies in their respective industries must never rest on their laurels. Apple today is one of the most popular tech consumer brands on earth, and its shift towards wearables and subscription services likely means it has a bright future, at least for the next decade. But no company is a true “buy and hold forever” investment, merely a “buy until the thesis breaks” one. Consumer tech is littered with examples of once-dominant phone makers (including Nokia (NYSE: NOK ), Motorola, and BlackBerry (NYSE: BB )) who took their customers for granted and thus were relegated to the ash heap of history.
What would the thesis be breaking on Apple entail? Well, for one thing, two to three consecutive years of earnings and FCF declines, as well as a sharp deceleration in service and “other” sales. Note that I’m not predicting this will necessarily happen anytime soon, just that investors should be on the lookout for these signs of trouble.
For the rest of this risk section, I want to point out that Apple, like all tech stocks, will experience normal stretches of sharp negative volatility. That’s because tech stocks, in general, have higher betas (volatility relative to the S&P 500):
1-year beta: 0.70 3-year beta: 1.22 5-year beta: 1.26 10-year beta: 1.29 Historical beta: 1.12 Even in the modern iPhone dominated (and slower growth) era, Apple shares can plunge nearly 30%, and that’s during a healthy economy and a secular bull market.
(Source: Ycharts)
Investors can expect a potentially much larger drop of 30% to 40% or possibly more during the next recession and overall bear market (for the S&P 500). That’s because the market will become obsessed with risks (what might go wrong with fundamentals), including how a recession might cause consumer spending on premium tech products to fall significantly. At such a time no matter how good the company’s actual results might be, shares will likely take it on the chin.
Apple’s last major bear market was also triggered by similar fear of “peak iPhone” which ultimately meant that it took the stock 18 months to recover to new all-time highs.
(Source: Ycharts)
I’m not necessarily expecting a repeat this time since every stock’s bear markets are slightly different. However, the point is that investors need to be prepared for flat returns for up to 12 to 24 months on Apple, which is a far cry from the stupendous returns over the past two years.
Just remember that periods of flat prices are the perfect time for long-term investors to steadily add to their positions. Since Apple’s earnings, free cash flow, and dividends are likely to keep growing steadily (though at a slower rate), the shares will steadily become more undervalued the longer its share price languishes. As long as the company’s fundamental business model remains intact (strong iOS ecosystem that’s steadily better monetized via services and wearables) Apple will remain one of the most attractive tech dividend growth blue-chips you can buy.
In fact, should the share price hang around current levels long enough, I will happily add Apple to my own high-yield dividend growth retirement portfolio, as the stock is on my bear market buy list with a target yield of 1.8%. That’s the yield at which I estimate that shares would generate 15+% CAGR total returns over the coming decade.
Bottom Line: Bear Markets On Quality Dividend Stocks Are The Best Time For Long-Term Investors To Buy
No one can predict the future, and so I can’t tell you whether or not Apple’s shares are done declining. In the short-term fickle market sentiment will dominate and Apple may very well have further to fall.
However, what I can tell you is that, despite what the stock’s recent plunge may seem to indicate, Apple’s long-term growth thesis is NOT broken. This is hardly the first time that “peak iPhone” fears have caused Apple shares to plunge. In fact, iPhone unit volumes actually peaked almost two years ago, and yet the company has managed to continue driving solid top and bottom line growth since then that’s resulted in excellent market-beating returns.
And while it’s true that Apple’s days of double-digit revenue growth are likely permanently behind it, we can’t forget that Apple remains one of the most profitable companies on earth. Specifically, the mountain of net cash it sits on ($123 billion) combined with its $50 billion in annual retained FCF, means that the company’s epic buyback program is going to continue for the foreseeable future. That, combined with its fast-growing wearables and service businesses, should allow the company to continue delivering double-digit EPS, FCF/share and dividend growth for many years to come.
Today Apple’s valuation, while not likely severely undervalued based on its realistic growth prospects, is good enough for me to recommend it to most investors. While I personally am waiting for a better yield to add it to my own portfolio, rest assured that I look forward to the day I can join the ranks of Apple’s shareholders. And the lower the stock falls, or the longer it languishes around current levels, the faster that day will come.
